headline: Blockchain smart contracts can prevent capital destruction in construction lending by enforcing payment covenants at the point of transaction rather than after insolvency
reasoning: Mitchell explains that in the Australian construction sector, when a builder collapses, the last one or two progress payments have typically already been spent across multiple sites, and subcontractors and suppliers beneath have not been paid. Traditional loan covenants that restrict use of funds can only be enforced through the courts, by which time the capital has already been dissipated. Smart contracts on blockchain enforce the rules in real time at the point of transaction, potentially preventing builders from trading while insolvent and protecting lenders and subcontractors from the cents-in-the-dollar outcomes common in construction insolvencies.
quote: Because typically when a builder goes under as, as anyone in the sector knows, they've been the last progress payment or the one and possibly the one before that, they're built in managing that across multiple sites. And it's likely that the subways and suppliers beneath haven't been paid. And, and this goes back to the point of our technology being able to enforce the rules around contracts in real time. So at the point of transaction, that's a brilliant part of smart contracts in blockchain tech because without that, you know, you can put it into a a contract, you can say the covenant says, you know, you can't use this in other, other projects. But by the time that that goes to be enforced in the courts, all the money's gone. You know, the capital's being torched, it's too late. So you're fighting over cents in the dollar in the courts rather than at the time of transaction that being enforced.
episode_title: From Bathla to blockchain: private credit faces transperancy test

headline: Australian REITs and real estate funds risk being disconnected from blockchain-based financial market infrastructure that US counterparts are actively preparing for
reasoning: Alistair Mitchell argues that in the US, 86% of institutional investors (per a Bank of New York survey) are preparing for blockchain-based financial market infrastructure, with JP Morgan, BlackRock and others leading the charge toward asset tokenisation. Larry Fink has stated every asset will be tokenised, and US real estate funds are already working toward that future by getting cash flows on-chain today. By contrast, Australian funds are not treating this as a priority, which Mitchell sees as a risk — in 5-10 years those that prepared will have unbreakable on-chain proof of assets and cash flows ready for tokenised trading, while those that didn't will be disconnected from these new financial rails.
quote: In the US, you see, you know, the biggest bank in the world, JP Morgan, the biggest asset manager in the world, BlackRock, both of those and and many other, you know, the Bank of New York, MD did a survey that says 86% of institutional investors in the US and now preparing for this future of blockchain based financial market infrastructure. You come to Australia and it's just not part of the conversation here. And I see this myself when I'm talking to to funds here who are looking to come on board our platform. Yes, they get the benefit of creating this immediate trust in their transactions, but they're not thinking about the future of having those transactions be part of this same piece of financial market infrastructure that those assets will be traded on in the future. Whereas in the US, this piece around what's called asset tokenization, which has been led by, you know, BlackRock and others, we have, Larry Fink has said that every asset will be tokenised into the future. That's the BlackRock road map. And in the US, all of the real estate funds are working towards that future.

headline: 'Great private credit redemption of 2026' underway globally as Bathla collapse exposes systemic transparency and information deficit across the sector
reasoning: Alistair Mitchell argues that most problems in private credit in 2026 trace back to either a lack of information or a lack of trust in the information provided to investors. The Bathla collapse — where a NSW property developer hid deposits from other lenders to obtain additional funding — exemplifies the opacity. ASIC has launched a significant investigation into the private credit sector and the RBA governor also flagged concerns. Investors are now withdrawing capital in what Mitchell calls the 'great private credit redemption of 2026', a global phenomenon seen in the US and Australia, with several Australian funds closing off redemptions. Investors can no longer accept the historical trade-off of higher returns in exchange for reduced transparency.
quote: I think the thing that all of these problems in private credit this year come back to is either a lack of information or a lack of trust in the information. So if we look at Baffa, for example, I mean, just one part of that story that made the headlines really stuck out to me, and that was his hidden email about the developer hiding certain deposits from other lenders so they could use that to get more funding from other lenders... bath has really been, I guess the, the, the moment where the tide went out and everyone's looking at who's, you know, wearing the skimpy swimsuit or nothing at all. And we've seen a number of funds in Australia now close off redemptions, for example. And so all of this comes back to what a private credit funds doing to give their investors confidence.

headline: Blockchain-based real-time transaction recording can close the information gap that is driving LP redemptions from private credit funds backing property developers
reasoning: Mitchell describes how his firm's technology sits between the movement of money in construction financing, mandating that developers and builders record every dollar in real time on a blockchain, creating a cryptographically signed, permanent, unbreakable and shareable record. This single source of truth is accessible to the entire economic chain — from on-site subcontractors all the way up to the superannuation fund LP in the private credit vehicle. He contrasts this with the current primitive back-office approach where duplicate paper receipts from two parties create a 'trust me' problem that banks cannot resolve due to privacy constraints. The technology also enforces contract covenants at the point of transaction via smart contracts, preventing, for example, developers from diverting restricted funds to other projects.
quote: the core of my business, we're a piece of technology that sits in between the movement of money. And in this construction example, private lenders mandate that the developer and the builders use our product so that every dollar of of money on that project is is recorded in real time. And we cryptographically sign that on a blockchain. And what that means is that every single dollar spent on that project is not only it's permanent, unbreakable and shareable at source record that's created. That means that the entire economic chain associated with that has access to that in real time. So right from the, you know, the sub here that's building the kitchen on site right through to the Dodger super fund, that might be the LP in the private credit fund that's funding the developer that's paying the builder.
